items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.description: Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century.

items.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
items.description: Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

items.title: 2026 Shorenstein Journalism Award: Shibani Mahtani on Democratic Backsliding in Southeast Asia
items.description: In her 15 years reporting on Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, Shibani Mahtani has witnessed the region’s once-vibrant press corps dwindle in size, as journalists are jailed, harassed, and sued by governments. This pressure, along with an industry-wide strain on the business of journalism, has forced many outlets to shutter. In her keynote address, she will discuss how this diminished media environment has had a profound impact on regional democracy at a time of seismic global instability and consider the challenges of navigating this reality.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections
items.description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Tradition as Method: The Minjung Art Movement and Decolonial Democracy in South Korea
items.description: In the 1970s and 1980s, dissident artists associated with South Korea's minjung (people's) art movement rejected both state-sponsored modernism and imported Cold War formalism. Yet their opposition to authoritarian rule did not entail a rejection of tradition. Instead, they turned to precolonial vernacular practices—Buddhist visual traditions, folk imagery, communal performance, and indigenous cultural practices—as critical resources for political expression.

items.title: Slavic Languages and Literatures: Bereza/Beryoze with Zozulka Trio
items.description: Many old songs brim with ecological awareness. Old songs from the territory of modern Ukraine tell stories about plants like the birch tree–bereza in Ukrainian, beryoze in Yiddish–that bend, break, and heal, becoming metaphors for human fragility and tenacity. Birds mark the turning of seasons and shifts in our internal weather as well. Since 2011, Zozulka–a trio named after the Ukrainian word for cuckoo bird–has interpreted songs from a wide range of Ukrainian village traditions. With BEREZA / BERYOZE, the trio branches into a new cycle of songs that speak directly to ecological themes.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Universal Human Psychology, "Bani Adam," and Our Omnicultural Future
items.description: “We’re all members of a whole sprung alike from a single soul; when one alone is struck with pain, the rest will feel the sharpest strain; if others’ woe leaves you unmoved, your humanity remains unproved.” (Translation Fathali Moghaddam/Duncan Wu) The above Farsi poem was written by the great Persian poet Saadi Shirazi (1210-1291). Bani Adam literally means the children of Adam. The poem describes the interconnected nature of humankind; we are all parts of the same whole, limbs belonging to one body. When one part of the body is in pain, then all the other limbs also suffer.

items.title: Branner Library Book & Map Exhibit - Water in the West
items.description: Branner Earth Sciences Library & Map Collection Exhibit: Water in the West Our Fall 2026 exhibition highlights the water resources in California & the Western United States to shed light on the issues that affect our waterways. The exhibit features maps and the Layperson’s guides series published by the Water Education Foundation, which aim to foster public understanding of water resources. These resources help inform collaborative decision-making to build collective solutions for water issues across the Western United States.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: The Fate of Earth
items.description: 🌎 Earth Systems Program 🌎 Please join us Friday, October 23, at 1 p.m. in Y2E2 299 for “The Fate of Earth,” a talk by Dr. Josh Fisher. Dr. Fisher uses satellite observations to explore how Earth’s ecosystems respond to a changing climate. His work spans more than a decade at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, where he helped establish the ECOSTRESS mission to study plant water use and stress from space. He now brings that expertise to research and teaching at Chapman University and satellite science at Hydrosat. Light refreshments will be provided. We hope you can join us!

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Book spells
items.description: Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell!

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
items.description: Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

items.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
items.description: Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents.

items.title: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection
items.description: In Focus: Asian American Art from the Collection showcases recent acquisitions made through the Cantor’s Asian American Art Initiative (AAAI), offering a glimpse into one of the fastest-growing areas of the museum’s collection. Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time. Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Book spells
items.description: Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell!

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
items.description: Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Branner Library Book & Map Exhibit - Water in the West
items.description: Branner Earth Sciences Library & Map Collection Exhibit: Water in the West Our Fall 2026 exhibition highlights the water resources in California & the Western United States to shed light on the issues that affect our waterways. The exhibit features maps and the Layperson’s guides series published by the Water Education Foundation, which aim to foster public understanding of water resources. These resources help inform collaborative decision-making to build collective solutions for water issues across the Western United States.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: The Golden Age’ or ‘the Dark Time of the Plots’: Iraq and Syria in the 1950s | Matthieu Rey
items.description: 1946. The last French soldier left Syria. A few months before, Tawfiq al-Suweidi, the Iraqi Prime Minister, introduced a set of laws to protect constitutional freedoms and legalize political parties. In both post-Ottoman countries, Iraq and Syria, the 1940s and 1950s were marked by a contradictory political legacy. On the one hand, parliaments ruled, political parties flourished, and civil society gained traction through public debate. On the other, emergency laws blocked debate, or the military interfered.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. items.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
items.description: Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

items.title: After Fission: Recognition and Contestation in the Atomic Age
items.description: About the event: Nuclear status is typically treated as a stable feature of a state's capacity to possess, use, or build nuclear weapons. Challenging this view, After Fission reveals how states contest their nuclear status in the atomic age. By examining the legal structure of the Non-Proliferation Treaty, technical ambiguities surrounding nuclear testing, and debates over rights and responsibilities in the global nuclear regime, Sidra Hamidi argues that a state's nuclear status is not simply a function of technical capability.

items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. items.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections
items.description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Book spells
items.description: Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell!

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century.

items.title: The Frontier Between Legendary Monsters and Verified Natural History
items.description: Have you ever looked at a mysterious lake shadow and thought, "Is that a giant prehistoric plesiosaur, or just an extraordinarily dramatic floating log?" If so, step into the corridors of the Science Library for our featured book display exploring where ancient myth meets rigorous evolutionary biology. We’re separating biological facts from blurry photographs, blurry folklore, and very clear hoaxes. Come for the ancient folklore, stay for the cold, hard science—and remember: the truth is in here, but so are the quiet study hours.

items.title: From Yahweh to Jupiter: Orthodox Muscovy Deals with the Classical World
items.description: Considering a few instances taking place between 1680–1705, the talk shows how interculturalism, multilingualism, and multiconfessionalism in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and in Ruthenia helped to spread Classical culture into Eastern Europe. In his collection, Multiflowered Garden (1680), the Belarusian Simiaon Polacki breaks with Orthodox skepticism towards ancient culture—deemed as sophistic—and includes references to Classical literature and mythology as signs of erudition and stylistic refinement to place the Slavic world in a line of continuity with the ancient one.

items.title: Korea’s Nuclear Odyssey Beyond Borders: From KEDO to the Age of AI
items.description: Every odyssey begins with a departure, but the Odyssey is also a story of return—not just to where one began, but to lessons learned along the way. South Korea’s nuclear journey beyond its borders spans three landmark projects: KEDO in North Korea, Barakah in the United Arab Emirates, and Dukovany in the Czech Republic. Each unfolded in a different international environment, from nonproliferation and energy cooperation to commercial competition and today’s renewed concerns over geopolitics and energy security. Dr.

items.title: SCRIPTA - Jutta Eming: A Sleeping Giant: The Transmission of the Sindbad / Seven Sages of Rome-Narrative
items.description: The Sindbad / Seven Sages of Rome-material is the most famous premodern narrative tradition of which nobody has ever heard. Told in at least 30 languages from Persia to Iceland over more than 10 centuries, the story cycle recounts a medieval #me-too story of a false rape accusation between a mute prince and his young stepmother at a royal court, and the impossibility of establishing the truth. As such, it is one of the most popular works of medieval and early modern literature.

items.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections
items.description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Worse than War: The Global Costs of Violence
items.description: About the event: Civil wars, interstate wars, and terrorism receive a great deal of media and policy attention, for good reasons. By contrast, the major forms of interpersonal violence—homicide, intimate partner violence, and severe physical punishment of children—generally have a much lower profile. In Worse than War, Anke Hoeffler and James Fearon assemble and analyze the data on the global prevalence and costs of collective and interpersonal violence. They show that interpersonal violence is vastly more widespread and imposes far greater societal costs than collective violence.

items.description: Abstract: From facial recognition—capable of checking people into flights or identifying undocumented residents—to automated decision systems that inform who gets loans and who receives bail, each of us moves through a world determined by data-empowered algorithms. But these technologies didn’t just appear: they are part of a history that goes back centuries, from the census enshrined in the US Constitution to the birth of eugenics in Victorian Britain to the development of Google search.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Book spells
items.description: Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell!

items.title: Branner Library Book & Map Exhibit - Water in the West
items.description: Branner Earth Sciences Library & Map Collection Exhibit: Water in the West Our Fall 2026 exhibition highlights the water resources in California & the Western United States to shed light on the issues that affect our waterways. The exhibit features maps and the Layperson’s guides series published by the Water Education Foundation, which aim to foster public understanding of water resources. These resources help inform collaborative decision-making to build collective solutions for water issues across the Western United States.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Rage Baiting and Border Crossing: How AI/LLMs Complicate Translation
items.description: Rage bait prompts audience engagement by provoking anger. Torsa Ghosal's talk compares “rage bait” narratives about border crossing generated by Large Language Models (LLMs) in two different languages: English and Bengali. Because LLMs are incapable of registering the cultural codes embedded in language, their mis-translations create problems, especially for non-English languages. Join us to discover how the spread of LLMs is impacting translation, migration narratives, and the preservation of world languages.

items.description: In honor of Prematurity Awareness Month in November, Univerity of California Milk Bank is partnering with UCSF Family Services to host a Human Milk Drive in support of premature and medically fragile infants. Human milk is the recommended source of nutrition for all infants and is especially critical for those born premature or medically fragile. When a mother’s own milk is not available, pasteurized donor human milk plays a vital role in filling this gap. If you’re a lactating parent with extra milk to share, your donation can make a meaningful difference.
